note: A full-text read of Carlo De Franceschi's «L'Istria: note storiche» (Parenzo, Gaetano Coana, 1879), from the Google scan held at the Internet Archive — 524 pages, searched end to end in September 2026. What follows is only what the book gives about this family's own places and name.
lead: Carlo De Franceschi is the family's historian, and until now this archive had used him second-hand: quoted in the Kandler literature, in the Blasonario, in Puhmajer's monograph on the Seget house. The book itself is online and free. Reading it whole does three things — it puts the family's home parishes into an ecclesiastical world nobody had described here, it gives the Seget estate a documented chain of owners and a list of the people who worked it, and it is conspicuously silent about the one thing the family most wants him to have said.

silence.heading: What the book does not say
silence.text: Carlo's own published history of Istria never claims the family came out of Carnia. The words Carnia and Cargna appear twice in 524 pages, both times about something else — a parish priest called «carnialico» who destroyed Roman inscriptions at S. Andrea, and a Latin tag about mortal flesh that the scanner's software misread. There is no passage on Friulian settlers named De Franceschi, no mention of Mione, Muina or Ovaro, and no origin story of any kind for his own family.
silence.why: This does not overturn the Carnia thesis. Carlo gave that account in his memoirs and in the letter this archive holds, not in this book, and a public history of the province is not where a nineteenth-century secretary of the provincial assembly would set down his own pedigree. But the archive has been treating Carlo as a single witness speaking with one voice, and he is not: the historian who published in 1879 and the man who wrote privately about his ancestors are the same person choosing to say different things in different places. Where the Carnia page says the claim is testimony and not record, that now has a sharper edge. See «Back to Carnia».
silence.detail: The one Friulian thread the book does carry is unrelated to the family: it describes the Furlan dialect of the interior as Roman speech fused with Carnic, and the road that brought Friulian soldiers, podestàs and merchants into Istria for four centuries.

pedena.heading: The diocese nobody had named
pedena.lead: Gallignana and Gologorica — the two parishes this archive's line runs through — were not in the diocese of Pisino. They were in the diocese of Pedena, the smallest in Istria, and Carlo lists it entire.
pedena.parishes: Pedena, Gallignana, Lindaro, Novacco, Cerovglie, Chersicla, Gollogorizza, Cherbune, Berdo, Cepich, S. Ivanaz, Grimalda — twelve parishes, with the vicariates of Sarez, Scopliaco, Grobnico, Previs, Tupliaco and Gradigne.

rows.lab: Gallignana held the only chapter
rows.text: Trieste had collegiate chapters at Muggia, Umago, Pinguente and Rozzo; Parenzo at Rovigno, Montona, Valle and four more; Pola at nine places. «Nella diocesi di Pedena unicamente a Gallignana con arciprete» — in the diocese of Pedena, at Gallignana alone, with an archpriest. Apart from the cathedral itself, the family's home parish was the ecclesiastical head of its diocese.

rows.lab: And it was a town, not a village
rows.text: In the Diet of the County of Pisino the bench of Communities seated only those places holding the title of città: Antignana, Bersez, Pedena, Gallignana, Lovrana and Pisino. Six. Gallignana sat in the prelates' bench too, through its chapter. The place the registers call a hill parish was one of six towns in the county, with two seats in its parliament.

rows.lab: A quarrel over the parish, 1324–1335
rows.text: The parish priest of Gallignana, Giovanni of Capodistria, died, and the bishop of Pedena failed to name a successor within the canonical term. Then the bishop died too. The vicar of the vacant diocese was Nicolò, pievano of Gollogorizza — the priest of this archive's other parish — and on 3 November 1324 he conferred the parish of Gallignana on a priest Cernaz of Pisino superiore. The patriarch Bertrando held the appointment void and ordered the abbot of Rosazzo to install Jacopo Sembiante instead, which happened on 24 March 1335. Eleven years, and the two parishes this line comes from are the two ends of the argument.

rows.lab: The bishops' own style
rows.text: The simple benefice of Gollogorizza was founded in 1444 by Currado Schuel, provost of Pisino. After its last holder, don Clemente Bioz, died, its revenues were assigned to the bishops of Pedena — and from then on those bishops signed themselves «Dominus Gollaegoritiae, Scopliaci et Tupliaci», Lord of Gologorica, Škopljak and Tupljak. A village of a few dozen houses is in a bishop's title.

rows.lab: What the bishops took
rows.text: At Gallignana the bishop drew half the fixed wine render called the episcopal census, and half the cheeses. At Pedena the whole tithe of grain, wine and lambs. The count of Pisino took the rest — money and animals.

rows.lab: Deeper than the church
rows.text: Carlo, following Kandler, reads the territory of the diocese of Pedena as the land of the Secussi, one of the Alpine peoples Pliny counted among the most illustrious of their neighbours: Chersicla, Grimalda, Previs, Bottonega, Sarez, Novaco, Cerovglie, Gollogorizza, Gradigne, Berdo, Carboneto, Scopuliano, Tupliano, Lindaro, Calliniana, Pedena, half of Gimino. Roman inscriptions carrying plain Roman names have been found at Gollogorizza, as at Bogliuno and Cepich. The two parishes are on ground that has been a unit since before the Romans arrived.

rows.w: In the Uskok War. Trautmannsdorff rushed a relief force from Gorizia under Don Baldassare Maradas, who attacked on 14 May and forced the Venetians back, took Fianona and Albona on the 20th — and, recalled to Gorizia, left Istria only after «assicurata Gallignana», securing Gallignana and reinforcing its garrison.

rows.t: Raiders strip the territory of Gollogorizza
rows.w: The Venetian captain Verzi, having burnt what was left of a village and killed an Uskok holding a house with ten countrymen, «scorse il territorio di Gollogorizza, ove predò 100 animali minuti ed alquanti grossi» — ran over the territory of Gologorica and took a hundred small beasts and a few large.

rows.t: The priest of Gallignana joins the Croatian Protestant press
rows.w: Francesco Claj, priest of Gallignana, contracted at Pisino with the reformers to revise and correct the Croatian translations, which he later declared exact. He offered to help only «rimanendo in patria» — on condition of staying home. The vicar of Pisino who signed with him, Matteo Zivcich, later turns up among the Lutheran preachers posted through the province.

rows.t: Bosnian and Morlach families settled at Gallignana
rows.w: Among the smaller resettlements — Gallignana, Pisino, Pisinvecchio, Lindaro, Zamasco and others took fewer than the big campaigns at Antignana, Corridico, Terviso, Vermo and Gimino.

seget.heading: Seget, in Carlo's own words
seget.lead: The archive already had the Cretan origin of the Seget branch from Petar Puhmajer's monograph. Here is the sentence Puhmajer is citing, in its place — and the footnote under it, which is worth more.
seget.quote: Il capitanio di Raspo Alessandro Zorzi in data 15 Febbraro 1604 investiva il capitano Vincenzo Cuchich da Sebenico d'un corpo di terreni incolti della circonferenza di circa quattro miglia nel territorio di Umago, sul quale furono da lui trasportate trenta famiglie da paesi turcheschi. Il Cuchich vendette nel 1623 la tenuta, che ora chiamasi di Seghetto e Giuba, ai N. U. Valier di Venezia, dai quali più tardi l'acquistò la nobile famiglia de Franceschi, attuale posseditrice, emigrata dall'isola di Candia dopo conquistata dai turchi nel 1669.
seget.trans: Alessandro Zorzi, captain of Raspo, on 15 February 1604 invested Captain Vincenzo Cuchich of Sebenico with a body of uncultivated land some four miles in circumference in the territory of Umago, onto which he brought thirty families from Turkish lands. Cuchich sold the estate — now called Seghetto and Giuba — in 1623 to the noble Valier of Venice, from whom it was later bought by the noble de Franceschi family, its present owner, emigrated from the island of Candia after the Turks conquered it in 1669.
seget.footnote: «Questa notizia la dobbiamo alla gentilezza del sig. Giambattista de Franceschi deputato al Consiglio dell'Impero, che la trasse dal proprio archivio domestico.» Carlo's source is not a chronicle. It is Giambattista de Franceschi — a deputy to the Imperial Council in Vienna — reading his own family's papers and passing them to a historian of the same surname. Two De Franceschi, one in parliament and one at the provincial assembly, settling their family's record between them in the 1870s.

list.heading: And the people who worked it: Seghetto di Umago, 30 April 1764
list.lead: Giambattista sent Carlo a second thing from that archive — the roll of colonist families then living on the estate, which Carlo prints entire. These are the descendants of Cuchich's thirty families. They are named, counted, and given their home cities, and every one of those cities is a place Venice had lost or was losing to the Ottomans.

rows.who: Giani de Marco, with his grandmother
Andrea de Nicola, with his brothers
Michiel de Giovo, with his mother and brothers

rows.from: origin not given — but the Lupatini were of Albona

list.close: A hundred and eleven people counted by name, plus three families whose provenance had already been forgotten by 1764. Carlo adds that other Greek families lived at Giuba — the Carciotti and the Stradiotti — and that the Melisana, Atica and Chitriza must have been foreigners too. Coron, Malvasia, Nauplia, Corinth, Arta: this is the Morea, emptied westward. The De Franceschi came from Crete to an estate already full of people who had come the same way.

elsewhere.w: A ducal grant licensed Leonardo Fioravanti, Sabba de Franceschi and Vincenzo dall'Acqua, Bolognese, to bring a hundred and twenty-four families to Pola to break new ground. They undertook to purify the air, uncover springs and introduce new methods of agriculture, and got twenty years free of taxes and military service, and two fairs to be held in the amphitheatre. The earliest bearer of the name in Istria this archive can date to a document, and he is neither Istrian nor Carnian.

Among the noble families living at Pola before the plague of 1631 — Locatelli, Dragoni, Sargo, Albini, Roberti, Cassinati, Barbabianca, Bolis, Marini, Franceschi (come from Capodistria), Forlani, Sozomeno. After the plague reduced the city to three hundred souls, these families either died out or settled elsewhere. A third, separate Franceschi arrival, by a third road.

sourcing: Two texts were used. The Internet Archive's Google scan of the 1879 Parenzo edition, item listrianotestor00frangoog, read through its OCR layer — which garbles accents, splits words and mangles the footnotes badly. And a clean transcription of several chapters published by istrianet.org from the Arnaldo Forni reprint, which the family has held since 2004 in its own files and which this archive did not open until it was pointed at it. Where the two disagree the transcription is followed, and the roll of 1764 above has been corrected against it — a dozen of the colonists' names were previously printed here in their OCR-mangled forms. Passages that survive only in the OCR are flagged as such in the text.

otherbook.heading: The other book — the one he dictated for a son who died
otherbook.lead: «L'Istria: note storiche» is the book Carlo published and the book this page has been reading. It is not the book that would answer this archive's questions. That one is «Memorie autobiografiche», and it was never printed in his lifetime, because — as a Trieste reviewer put it in 1926 — «Impossibile sarebbe stato il pensarne la pubblicazione sotto l'Austria». It would have been impossible to think of publishing it under Austria.

rows.lab: What it is, and when he made it
rows.text: «Le Memorie sono scritte in forma di lettere, ché dall'aprile al dicembre 1883, l'illustre storiografo istriano, già settuagenario, dettava per compiacere al desiderio del figlio Giampietro, morto immaturamente un anno dopo.» The Memoirs are written as letters, dictated between April and December 1883 by the historian, already in his seventies, to satisfy the wish of his son Giampietro — who died prematurely a year later.

rows.lab: And the archive has the son's grave
rows.text: On the right-hand tablet of the family tomb at Gologorica, photographed this year: «PIETRO fu CARLO / MAGISTRATO / ROVIGNO 1854 — MONCALVO 1884». Born at Rovigno in 1854, dead at Moncalvo in 1884. A newspaper in Trieste in 1926 and a stone in an Istrian village churchyard, and they say the same thing: the son asked, the father spent nine months dictating his life, and the son was dead within the year. The book exists because of him.

rows.lab: Camillo published it, and annotated it heavily
rows.text: It appeared for the first time in the 1926 volume of the «Archeografo Triestino», the review of the Società di Minerva, edited by Carlo's other son Camillo — who added not only a preface «dove con serenità di storico delinea il ritratto e l'opera del padre», drawing his father's portrait and work with a historian's composure, but over a hundred notes. It was also sold separately by booksellers, which is why copies circulate as a book of about three hundred pages.

rows.lab: What the reviewer says is in it
rows.text: An intimate view of Istrian political life from the first decades of the nineteenth century almost to its close. His father and his uncle still held to the old devotion to the Empire; he was the Risorgimento generation. At Graz he read nothing but Italian authors and talked so boldly that his landlady predicted the gallows for him. As a judicial official he was under the eye of the captain of Pisino, Baron Grimschitz. In 1848 the Istrian electors sent him to the Vienna Parliament with Madonizza, Vidulich and Fachinetti; he saw the October revolution, the siege and the bombardment, and «di quei tragici giorni ci dà nelle Memorie una descrizione drammaticissima, che basterebbe essa sola alla fama del libro» — of those tragic days he gives a description dramatic enough on its own to make the book's reputation.

rows.lab: Then the cost of it
rows.text: Back at his obscure post in Rovigno he lasted until 1854, when he was thrown out with a pension so poor he could be called destitute. He took refuge at Fiume, living in a generous lawyer's office until 1860, keeping up the historical and archaeological work that had made him Kandler's collaborator. When the constitution was restored, the Diet of Parenzo — «la famosa Dieta del Nessuno», the famous Diet of Nobody, which refused to send deputies to Vienna — called the exile to be its secretary. Offered a rise on his meagre salary, he refused it out of regard for the province's poor finances, and went on living «pur carico di famiglia, nella voluta povertà» — burdened with a family, in chosen poverty. The Government opposed every candidature he stood for.

rows.lab: And a date it settles, and one it gets wrong
rows.text: «Carlo De Franceschi nacque il 1809 in Moncalvo, un umile villaggio della contea di Pisino.» Born 1809 — which is what his own tomb says, MDCCCIX, and what this archive published against a newspaper obituary of 1893 that gave 1810. But the same review has him dying «l'8 gennaio 1898», and that is wrong: he died on 8 January 1893, as the tomb, the obituaries and the whole of this archive agree. The day and month are right and a digit has slipped. Printed sources make this mistake too, which is the point of checking them.

otherbook.want: So: this archive does not have the «Memorie autobiografiche», and should. It is Carlo in the first person, at seventy-four, on his own family, his own village and his own century, with a hundred notes by the son who spent his life on the family's history. Everything on this site about Carlo has been assembled from the outside — from Kobler's correspondence, from the Istrian press, from a monograph, from his tomb. The book in which he speaks for himself has been in print since 1926.
otherbook.source_other: «Il Piccolo» of Trieste, 24 April 1926, page 3, reviewing the 1926 volume of the «Archeografo Triestino»; noticed also in «Il Piccolo» of 16 April 1926. Both read from the Internet Archive's run of the paper, September 2026. The book: Carlo De Franceschi, «Memorie autobiografiche», with preface, notes and appendices by Camillo De Franceschi, Archeografo Triestino / Lloyd Triestino, Trieste 1926, about 300 pp. The bibliography of Carlo's works is from istrianet.org.

found.heading: And then it was found, free, in an afternoon
found.lead: The section above was written saying this archive did not have the «Memorie autobiografiche» and should. It now has them. The whole book is open access at OpenStarts, the institutional repository of the University of Trieste, which has digitised the «Archeografo Triestino» entire: 309 pages, handle 10077/24521, no login, no charge. A first read gives the following, and there is a great deal more in it.

rows.lab: His grandfather and his great-uncle, and what the uncle did in 1809
rows.text: Camillo, on where his father's politics did not come from: «Non le assorbì certo in famiglia, dove tanto il padre Giuseppe che lo zio Giacomo ostentavano sentimenti di tenace attaccamento all'Austria e a Francesco I.» He certainly did not absorb them at home, where both his father Giuseppe and his uncle Giacomo made a show of stubborn attachment to Austria and to Francis I. And then: «Giacomo De Franceschi aveva preso parte attiva alla preparazione dell'insurrezione istriana del 1809 contro i Francesi, soffocata nel sangue», and with two other representatives of the County — the young Triestine Antonio Dietrich, later a lieutenant field marshal, and Ivancich of Pisino — had gone to Rovigno. Giacomo De Franceschi helped prepare the Istrian rising of 1809 against the French, and it was drowned in blood.

rows.lab: Carlo was born a French citizen
rows.text: «Era nato cittadino francese, tre giorni dopo la cessione della Contea di Pisino alla Francia, ed egli soleva dire scherzosamente d'avere nutrito dalla culla le idee liberali e democratiche della grande Rivoluzione.» He was born a French citizen, three days after the County of Pazin was ceded to France, and used to say jokingly that he had been fed the liberal and democratic ideas of the great Revolution from the cradle. So the man who spent his life asserting the Italianness of Istria was, for the first weeks of it, a subject of Napoleon — and knew it, and made a joke of it.

rows.lab: Which settles a date, by arithmetic
rows.text: Camillo opens by saying his father was born «il 16 ottobre 1809». The Gologorica baptism register, which this archive read from the microfilm, gives 17 October 1809, house 17. Camillo's own «three days after the cession» is the tie-breaker: the Treaty of Schönbrunn was signed on 14 October 1809, and three days after that is the 17th, not the 16th. The register stands. A son writing in 1926 was a day out, and his own sentence catches it.

rows.lab: The son the book was written for
rows.text: «Furono da lui scritte per compiacere al desiderio e alle insistenti richieste del figlio Gian Pietro, aggiunto giudiziale in Pola, giovane di promettente ingegno e di felici attitudini letterarie, morto immaturamente a trenta anni nel 1884.» Written to satisfy the wish and the insistent asking of his son Gian Pietro, assistant judge at Pola, a young man of promising talent and happy literary gifts, dead prematurely at thirty in 1884. The tomb at Gologorica says PIETRO fu CARLO, MAGISTRATO, Rovigno 1854 — Moncalvo 1884. Thirty exactly. And Camillo adds that Gian Pietro, before he died, left the manuscript to his two brothers.

rows.lab: What Carlo thought he was writing
rows.text: «Gettate giù in fretta e alla buona, spesso senza ordine e successione cronologica dei fatti, non essendo in origine destinate alla pubblicità, ma considerate come semplici scritti confidenziali di padre a figlio.» Thrown down in haste and plainly, often out of order, never meant for publication — simple confidential writings from a father to a son. Which is why they are worth more than the book he did publish.

rows.lab: The village, as his son saw it
rows.text: «Nato nell'umile sperduto villaggio di Moncalvo, dell'antica Contea di Pisino, in faccia al superbo panorama del Monte Maggiore e della Valle dell'Arsa … mentre a destra si profilano sull'orizzonte i monti di Pedena, Gallignana, Lindaro, con le vette segnate dagli agili campanili veneti di pietra bianca.» Born in the humble lost village of Moncalvo in the old County of Pazin, facing the Monte Maggiore and the Arsa valley, with the hills of Pedena, Gallignana and Lindar on the horizon to the right, their summits marked by slender Venetian bell-towers of white stone. Every place-name in that sentence is a place this archive has been reading registers from.

rows.lab: And the first history lesson of his life
rows.text: Coming home from his first year at the gymnasium at Fiume, riding with his father, they stopped at Passo on the Monte Maggiore road with «il parroco Ierbulla di Gallignana, uomo colto e patriotta» — the parish priest of Gallignana, a cultivated and patriotic man — who asked the boy whether he had studied any history. He managed Pola, Nesactium, and a battle near Lovran. The priest told him that among the ancient Istrian cities there was also Faveria, whose remains he said were at Čepić by Lake Arsa. «Queste le mie prime notizie di storia istriana» — these were my first pieces of Istrian history. The historian of Istria got his start from the parish priest of the town whose baptism book this archive has just finished reading.

rows.lab: And the cost, in his son's words
rows.text: «Con tutti i suoi talenti ed i suoi meriti, condusse una vita stentata e morì povero.» A family of seven mouths and two sons kept at their studies away from home; eleven years in the service of the Istrian Provincial Committee on twelve hundred florins without a single rise, because he had refused to sign the officials' petition for one, so as not to unbalance the provincial budget. And Baron Federico Grimschitz, captain of Istria, kept a black book of Istrians politically dangerous — «in cui apparivano annotate oltre quattrocento persone», with more than four hundred people entered in it.

found.more: This is one afternoon's reading of a book of three hundred and nine pages, and the search terms that failed are as telling as the ones that worked: «Carnia» does not appear in it at all, «Gologorica» not once — the village is always Moncalvo — and neither does the year 1711 nor the name Leonardo in any family sense. So the Memorie do not, on a first pass, answer the question this archive most wants answered. Carlo wrote about his century, not about his descent. But there are a hundred notes by Camillo, appendices, and the whole of the narrative still to read properly, and Camillo was the family's own historian.
found.also: Two more came off the same shelf at Trieste in the same minutes, both open access, neither previously held here. Francesco Salata, «Un precursore: Carlo De Franceschi», the address given at Pisino on 23 June 1929 with notes and documents, 52 pages, handle 10077/23581. And «A Carlo De Franceschi, dedicandogli Pisino pubblico busto bronzeo» of 1928, 110 pages, handle 10077/23559 — which carries a preface, a bibliography of his published writings, and «lettere di Carlo De Franceschi a Pietro Kandler e ad altri». Letters to Kandler and to others: a body of his correspondence this archive knew existed in the Zagreb boxes and did not know was in print.
found.source_found: Carlo De Franceschi, «Memorie autobiografiche», with preface, notes and appendices by Camillo De Franceschi, «Archeografo Triestino», Serie III vol. XII (XL), 1925–26, 309 pp. Open access at OpenStarts, Università degli Studi di Trieste, hdl.handle.net/10077/24521. Downloaded and read 7 September 2026.

antoljak.heading: A hundred years later, a Croatian historian argues with him for forty-six pages
antoljak.lead: David handed this archive a 475-page book on 9 September 2026: Stjepan Antoljak, «Hrvati u prošlosti» — Croats in the Past — a collected volume by one of the leading Croatian medievalists of the twentieth century. It had never been read here. Its index has an entry for **«Franceschi de, C.»** with sixteen page references, and what it shows is something this archive had not been able to show before: not that Carlo is cited, but what happens when a serious opponent takes him seriously.

rows.lab: He is a source on every page of the Slav settlement chapter
rows.text: Antoljak's long study of when and how the Slavs came into Istria cites **«C. De Franceschi, L'Istria: note storiche, Parenzo 1879»** twenty-one times, at pages 24, 25, 33, 38, 41, 45, 47–49, 52, 57, 59, 60, 62, 64, 66 and 70 — and also his 1852 article «Sulle varie popolazioni dell'Istria» in the Trieste paper «L'Istria». He is quoted for the date Istria fell to Byzantium (539), for Belisarius, for the charter of 1234 that names a «monte Schiavo» opposite Brtonigla, for the road called the «callis sclavonica», for the chronology of the Lombard and Avar raids. He is used exactly as a modern historian uses a nineteenth-century authority: constantly, and never quite trusted.

rows.lab: And Antoljak catches him out
rows.text:
«…a drugim se navodom De Franceschija da u listini iz iste godine piše *Villa Sclavorum de Longera*, naprosto ne može poslužiti jer je **netočno pročitan** i tako iznesen.» — De Franceschi's other citation, that a document of the same year reads *Villa Sclavorum de Longera*, simply cannot serve, because it was **misread** and reported that way.

The archive should say plainly what that is. It is the same failure this project keeps finding in its own work: a document read at speed, transcribed wrong, and then argued from. Carlo did it in print in 1879 and it was still being corrected ninety years later.

rows.lab: The hard one, and it belongs on this page
rows.text:
«**C. De Franceschi 1885. godine toliko se zaboravlja** kada piše da povijest pokazuje da Istra nije bila nikada zauzeta od nekog slavenskog naroda ili da je takav njom vladao.»

— *In 1885 C. De Franceschi so far forgets himself as to write that history shows Istria was never occupied by any Slav people, nor ruled by one.*

Antoljak goes on: that although Carlo uses Constantine Porphyrogenitus, he interprets him to suit himself; that he asserts the Croats never crossed the border of Istria and spread only as far as the river «Tarsia» — **and that Carlo has confused the Rječina at Rijeka with the Arsia, the Raša**, which is a different river eighty kilometres away and the whole point of the argument.

This archive has called Carlo the family's historian and leaned on him for the Carnian origin, and will go on doing both. It should also say this. On the national question he was a partisan of the Italian side of a bitter argument, and he was wrong in a way a specialist could demonstrate from the sources he himself was using. Being wrong there does not make him wrong about his own family's origin — a man is a better witness to his great-grandfather's house than to the seventh century. But it is the reason this archive tests him rather than quotes him.

rows.lab: «prilično oprezni De Franceschi»
rows.text: Not all of it is against him. Elsewhere Antoljak calls him «prilično oprezni De Franceschi» — the fairly cautious De Franceschi — for declining to credit an early Slav presence that other writers assert freely. The same man, in the same book, is both the careless reader and the cautious one. That is what a real reputation looks like at a hundred years' distance.

antoljak.source: Stjepan Antoljak, «Hrvati u prošlosti: izabrani radovi», Književni krug, Split 1992 (the ABBYY-scanned PDF David supplied, 475 pp.). Index entry «Franceschi de, C.», p. 24 ff.; the criticisms at pp. 33 and 45–47 of the printed pagination.
